name: app.R
content:
library(shiny)

cases <- list(
  list(title="1. Triage: The Diabetes Clinic Dataset", icon="🩺",
       story="The Diabetes Research Clinic has recruited patients with Type 2 diabetes into a study investigating risk factors for poor glucose control. Before the researchers can analyse the data, they need your help. Patient records must be checked for mistakes, missing information, and unusual values that could distort the results. Your first task is to review the patient data and make sure it is suitable for analysis.",
       evidence="A research nurse has recorded the HbA1c (%) results for eight patients with Type 2 diabetes: 6.4, 6.8, 7.0, 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 7.5, 12.8. The research team wants a summary value that is not overly influenced by the unusually high HbA1c result.", unlock="The patient records have been checked and summarised. Next, investigate how well the new screening test identifies Type 2 diabetes.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="Which measure is usually less affected by an unusually high HbA1c value?", choices=c("Mean"="mean","Median"="median","Range"="range","Standard deviation"="sd"), answer="median", hint="Think about the measure that depends on the middle value(s) rather than every value in the dataset.", explanation="The median is less affected by extreme values because it depends on the middle of the ordered data."),
         Medium=list(question="What is the median HbA1c (%) of these eight patients?", choices=c("7.0%"="7.0","7.15%"="7.15","7.2%"="7.2","7.5%"="7.5"), answer="7.15", hint="There are eight values, so find the two middle observations and calculate their average.", explanation="The middle values are 7.1 and 7.2. Median = (7.1 + 7.2) / 2 = 7.15%. The median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order."),
         Hard=list(question="A laboratory report lists an HbA1c result of 20%. What should the research team do?", choices=c("Delete the value immediately"="delete","Replace it with the sample mean"="replace","Check whether it is a data-entry or recording blunder before deciding what to do."="check"), answer="check", hint="An implausible value may be a recording error, but it should be investigated before any decision is made.", explanation="Data should be screened before analysis to identify possible blunders and outliers. A value of 20% is highly suspicious and should be checked against the original record before any decision is made.")),
       recovery_question="Why do statisticians screen a dataset before analysing it?", recovery_choices=c("To identify mistakes, unusual values, and missing data."="yes","To guarantee statistically significant results."="no","To make every variable Normally distributed."="normal"), recovery_answer="yes"),
  
  list(title="2. Diabetes Screening Unit", icon="🧪",
       story="The diabetes research team is planning a community screening programme to identify people at risk of Type 2 diabetes. Not everyone with risk factors will develop the condition, so researchers use probability to describe uncertainty and estimate the likelihood of different outcomes. Can you help the team interpret the numbers?",
       evidence="A research study followed 200 patients over five years to investigate the relationship between pre-diabetes and the development of Type 2 diabetes. Of the 100 patients with pre-diabetes, 20 developed Type 2 diabetes. Of the 100 patients without pre-diabetes, 5 developed the condition. The research team wants to use these results to compare the probability of developing Type 2 diabetes between the two groups.", unlock="You’ve compared the probabilities of developing Type 2 diabetes. Next, the research team will use a sample to estimate blood pressure across a wider population.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="A probability must lie within which range? ", choices=c("From -1 to 1"="minus","From 0 to 1 inclusive"="inclusive","From 1 to 100"="hundred","It can be any real number"="real"), answer="inclusive", hint="A probability of 0 means an event cannot happen, and a probability of 1 means an event is certain to happen.", explanation="Correct, probabilities always fall between 0 and 1, including the endpoints."),
         Medium=list(question="Based on the data, if you don’t have pre-diabetes, what is the probability of developing Type 2 diabetes within five years?", choices=c("2.5%"="2.5","5%"="5","10%"="10","15%"="15"), answer="5", hint="Look only at the patients without pre-diabetes. Divide the number who developed diabetes by the total number in this group.", explanation="Of the 100 patients without pre-diabetes, 5 developed Type 2 diabetes within five years. Therefore, the probability is 5%."),
         Hard=list(question="Based on the data, if you have pre-diabetes, what is the probability of developing Type 2 diabetes within five years?", choices=c("5%"="5","10%"="10","15%"="15","20%"="20"), answer="20", hint="Look only at the patients who have pre-diabetes. Divide the number who developed diabetes by the total number in this group.", explanation="Out of the 100 patients who had pre-diabetes, 20 developed Type 2 diabetes within five years.")),
       recovery_question="If P(A) = 0.2, what is the probability that A does not occur?", recovery_choices=c("0.2"="a","0.8"="b","1.2"="c"), recovery_answer="b"),
  
  list(title="3. Diabetes Research Unit: Learning from a Sample", icon="📋",
       story="The diabetes research team wants to estimate the average systolic blood pressure of adults with Type 2 diabetes attending clinics in Northern Ireland. Measuring every patient is impossible, so the researchers select a sample and use it to estimate the population mean. The team also wants to understand how certain they can be about that estimate.",
       evidence="The researchers randomly selected 120 adults with Type 2 diabetes. The sample mean systolic blood pressure was 132 mmHg. Blood pressure varies between individuals, so the sample mean is only an estimate of the population mean. Confidence intervals help researchers describe the uncertainty around that estimate.", unlock="You’ve explored sampling and uncertainty. Now investigate whether patient characteristics are associated with Type 2 diabetes.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="What is a sample?", choices=c("Every person with Type 2 diabetes in Northern Ireland."="NI","A subset of the population"="subset","A population parameter."="parameter","A confidence interval."="interval"), answer="subset", hint="A sample is a smaller group chosen from the population we want to learn about.", explanation="A sample is the smaller group of individuals selected from the population. Researchers use information from this group to estimate characteristics of the whole population. Random selection can help reduce selection bias, although it does not guarantee that every sample will perfectly represent the population."),
         Medium=list(question="What generally happens to a confidence interval when sample size increases, assuming everything else stays the same?", choices=c("It becomes narrower."="narrow","It becomes wider"="wide","It must contain every observation."="every","It becomes identical to the population range."="population"), answer="narrow", hint="A bigger sample usually provides more precise estimates because the standard error becomes smaller.", explanation="The standard error is calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size. As the sample size increases, the standard error decreases. This generally produces a narrower confidence interval and a more precise estimate of the population mean."),
         Hard=list(question="A 95% confidence interval for the mean systolic blood pressure is calculated repeatedly using the same method on many random samples. Which interpretation is correct?", choices=c("95% of individual blood pressure values lie in every interval"="a","95% of intervals calculated this way capture the population mean in repeated sampling."="b","The sample mean has a 95% chance of being inside its own interval."="c","The population parameter changes from sample to sample."="d"), answer="b", hint="Imagine repeating the same diabetes study many times using different random samples from the same population. What proportion of the intervals would be expected to contain the fixed population mean?", explanation="The correct interpretation is that if the same sampling method were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the confidence intervals calculated would contain the true population mean. The population mean is fixed, but the interval changes from sample to sample. This does not mean that 95% of individual patients' blood pressure measurements lie within the interval.")),
       recovery_question="A sample statistic is used to estimate what?", recovery_choices=c("A population parameter"="parameter","A guaranteed future result"="future","The measurement instrument"="instrument"), recovery_answer="parameter"),
  
  list(title="4. Diabetes Clinical Trial: Does the new treatment work?", icon="🧬",
       story="The diabetes research team has completed a clinical trial comparing a new glucose-lowering medication with standard care. After 12 months, the researchers recorded whether patients achieved their target HbA1c level. Now they must decide whether the differences observed between the treatment groups are convincing evidence that the new treatment is effective, or whether the results could simply be due to chance. This is where hypothesis testing becomes important.",
       evidence="Researchers compared two groups of patients with Type 2 diabetes. In the new-treatment group, 35 of 60 patients reached the target HbA1c level. In the standard-treatment group, 57 of 140 patients reached the target. The research team wants to determine whether the difference in the proportions reaching the target provides evidence of a treatment difference. Use the interactive tool below to carry out a chi-squared test at the 5% significance level.", unlock="You’ve interpreted a hypothesis test comparing two independent treatment groups. Next, choose the appropriate statistical tests for different study designs.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="Which test is commonly used to compare proportions between two groups?", choices=c("Chi-squared test"="chi","Independent-samples t-test"="t","Pearson correlation"="correlation","One-sample t-test"="one"), answer="chi", hint="The outcome is categorical: each patient either reached the HbA1c target or did not. The two treatment groups contain different patients.", explanation="A chi-squared test is appropriate for comparing proportions between two independent groups when the outcome is categorical. Here, the null hypothesis is that the proportion reaching the HbA1c target is the same in the new-treatment and standard-treatment groups."),
         Medium=list(question="Use the interactive tool below to calculate the p-value for the difference in the proportions reaching the HbA1c target. At the 5% significance level, what decision should the researchers make?", choices=c("Reject the null hypothesis."="reject","Accept the null hypothesis."="accept","Prove that the alternative is true."="prove","Ignore the result"="ignore"), answer="reject", hint="Compare the p-value with the 5% significance level (0.05). If the p-value is smaller than 0.05, the result is statistically significant.", explanation="The chi-squared test gives a p-value of approximately 0.022. Since 0.022 is below 0.05, the researchers reject the null hypothesis. There is statistically significant evidence that the proportions reaching the HbA1c target differ between the two treatment groups. This does not, by itself, establish whether the treatment is clinically worthwhile."),
         Hard=list(question="The new treatment produces a statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients reaching the HbA1c target. However, the drug is extremely expensive and frequently causes side effects. Which statement is most appropriate?", choices=c("Statistical significance guarantees the treatment should be used."="stat","Benefits, harms, and costs must also be considered"="cost","A significant result proves the treatment will work for every patient."="everyone","A p-value alone establishes the best treatment."="alone"), answer="cost", hint="A p-value tells us how strong the evidence is against the null hypothesis. It does not automatically tell us whether the effect is worthwhile in practice.", explanation="Statistical significance provides evidence that the observed difference is unlikely to be explained by chance alone under the null hypothesis. It does not show whether the size of the benefit is large enough to matter to patients. Clinical decisions should also consider the magnitude of the benefit, side effects, patient preferences, and cost. A statistically significant result is not automatically clinically important.")),
       recovery_question="What is the null hypothesis in a chi-squared test of independence?", recovery_choices=c("The variables are associated"="associated","There is no association between the variables"="independent","One variable causes the other"="cause"), recovery_answer="independent"),
  
  list(title="5. Diabetes Treatment Evaluation", icon="⚖️",
       story="The diabetes research team is now analysing data from several studies. Some research questions involve comparing patient results with a known reference value. Others compare two different treatment groups, while some involve measuring the same patients before or after treatment. To help the team reach the correct conclusion, you must choose the most appropriate statistical test for each situation.",
       evidence="Researchers have collected three diabetes datasets: 1. A sample of patients with Type 2 diabetes compared with an HbA1c target value of 7.0%; 2. Two separate groups of patients who received two different diabetes medications; 3. The same patients tested for their HbA1c levels before and after a lifestyle intervention. Different study designs require different hypothesis tests.", unlock="You’ve matched the test to the study design. Next, compare blood pressure across more than two BMI groups.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="A researcher wants to determine whether the mean HbA1c in a sample of patients differs from the recommended target value of 7.0%. Which test is most appropriate?", choices=c("One-sample t-test"="one","Independent-samples t-test"="independent","Paired-samples t-test"="paired","Chi-squared test"="chi"), answer="one", hint="The sample mean is being compared with a single reference value, rather than with another group.", explanation="A one-sample t-test compares the mean of one sample with a known or specified reference value. Here, it can be used to assess whether the mean HbA1c differs from the 7.0% target."),
         Medium=list(question="Researchers want to compare the mean HbA1c level between the two groups. Which test is most appropriate?", choices=c("Paired-samples t-test"="paired","Independent-samples t-test"="independent","One-sample t-test"="one","Spearman rank correlation"="spearman"), answer="independent", hint="The two groups contain different patients, and you are comparing their mean HbA1c levels.", explanation="An independent-samples t-test compares the mean HbA1c levels of two separate groups of patients."),
         Hard=list(question="Researchers record HbA1c in the same patients before starting a weight-loss programme and again six months later. Which feature of this scenario makes a paired-samples t-test appropriate?", choices=c("There are two different independent groups"="independent","The two measurements are linked within each patient"="linked","The outcome is nominal"="nominal","There are three or more independent groups"="three"), answer="linked", hint="Think about where the second measurement came from.", explanation="A paired-samples t-test is used when two measurements are linked or paired. In this study, each patient's follow-up HbA1c measurement is paired with their own baseline HbA1c measurement.")),
       recovery_question="Which test compares the means of two independent groups when the outcome is continuous and assumptions are met?", recovery_choices=c("Independent-samples t-test"="independent","Paired-samples t-test"="paired","One-sample t-test"="one"), recovery_answer="independent"),
  
  list(title="6. Diabetes Research Laboratory: When assumptions fail", icon="🧫",
       story="The diabetes research team is expanding their investigation. Some laboratory variables are highly skewed, making standard parametric tests unsuitable. Your challenge is to choose the most appropriate method when the usual assumptions are not met. Non-parametric methods can provide a better solution when data is skewed or when Normality assumptions fail.",
       evidence="The team is working with three diabetes datasets: 1. Urinary biomarker levels are highly skewed in patients with Type 2 diabetes and healthy control subjects; 2. HbA1c is measured before and after a weight-management programme in the same patients, but the differences are highly skewed; 3. Three different treatments are compared using HbA1c reduction, and the data are strongly skewed.", unlock="The laboratory analysis is complete. In the final room, use age and BMI together to investigate the probability of Type 2 diabetes.",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="Researchers want to compare a highly skewed biomarker level between patients with Type 2 diabetes and healthy control subjects. Which test is most appropriate?", choices=c("Independent-samples t-test"="independent","Paired t-test"="paired","Mann-Whitney U test"="mann","Pearson correlation"="correlation"), answer="mann", hint="The groups are independent and the data is not Normally distributed.", explanation="The Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric alternative to the independent-samples t-test. It is useful when data is skewed or when Normality assumptions are not satisfied."),
         Medium=list(question="Three independent diabetes treatment groups are being compared using HbA1c reduction. The data are strongly skewed and the usual ANOVA assumptions are not met. Which method is most appropriate?", choices=c("One-sample t-test"="one","Independent-samples t-test"="independent","Kruskal-Wallis test"="kw","Spearman correlation"="spearman"), answer="kw", hint="There are more than two independent groups, and the usual ANOVA assumptions are not met.", explanation="The Kruskal-Wallis test is a non-parametric method for comparing three or more independent groups. It is a suitable alternative when the assumptions for one-way ANOVA are not met."),
         Hard=list(question="The same patients have HbA1c measured before and after a lifestyle intervention.  The within-patient differences are strongly skewed and Normality assumptions are not satisfied. Which test is most appropriate?", choices=c("Independent-samples t-test"="independent","Mann-Whitney U test"= "mann","Paired-samples t-test"="pair","Wilcoxon signed-rank test"="wil"), answer="wil", hint="The measurements are paired because they come from the same patient, but the paired t-test assumptions are not met.", explanation="The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric alternative to the paired-samples t-test. It is used when paired measurements are available but the differences are not Normally distributed.")),
       recovery_question="What is a non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA for three or more independent groups?", recovery_choices=c("Kruskal–Wallis test"="kw","Paired t-test"="paired","Pearson correlation"="pearson"), recovery_answer="kw"),
  
  list(title="7. Final Data Room: Predicting Diabetes Risk", icon="📈",
       story="You’ve reached the final stage of the investigation. The research team wants to use patient information to estimate the likelihood of Type 2 diabetes. They are interested in how age and BMI contribute to risk. Your task is to explore a binary logistic regression model and understand how it produces a predicted probability.",
       evidence="The outcome recorded for each patient is whether Type 2 diabetes is present (yes/no). Age and BMI are used as predictor variables. The model combines these measurements to estimate the probability that the patient has Type 2 diabetes. In this teaching example, the model is: logit(p) = -8 + 0.04 × Age + 0.12 × BMI. These coefficients are illustrative teaching values, not estimates from a validated clinical model. A positive coefficient means that, with the other variable held constant, a higher value of that predictor increases the model's estimated log-odds of diabetes. The model converts these log-odds into a predicted probability. It is not a validated clinical risk tool, and a predicted probability is not a diagnosis.", unlock="You’ve finished all seven stages!",
       levels=list(
         Easy=list(question="Why is binary logistic regression suitable when predicting whether a patient has Type 2 diabetes?", choices=c("The outcome has two categories: diabetes present or absent."="binary","The outcome is always a continuous measurement."="continuous","It proves that age causes diabetes."="cause","It compares the means of three groups."="means"), answer="binary", hint="Think about the two possible outcomes recorded for each patient.", explanation="Binary logistic regression is used when the outcome has two categories, such as Type 2 diabetes present or absent. The model estimates the probability of one of those outcomes."),
         Medium=list(question="In the model logit(p) = -8 + 0.04 × Age + 0.12 × BMI, what does the positive BMI coefficient indicate?", choices=c("Holding age constant, higher BMI increases the model's estimated probability of diabetes."="positive","Higher BMI guarantees that a patient has diabetes."="guarantee","BMI has no relationship with the model prediction."="none","The probability must increase by exactly 12 percentage points for each BMI unit."="twelve"), answer="positive", hint="The coefficient is positive, but it does not represent a direct percentage-point change in probability.", explanation="The positive coefficient means that, holding age constant, a higher BMI increases the model's estimated log-odds and therefore its predicted probability of diabetes. It does not mean the probability rises by a fixed 12 percentage points per BMI unit."),
         Hard=list(question="A patient’s modelled probability of having Type 2 diabetes is 72%. Which is the most appropriate interpretation?", choices=c("The model estimates a 72% probability, but this does not confirm a diagnosis."="estimate","The patient definitely has diabetes."="certain","There is a 72% chance that BMI caused diabetes."="cause","The model is 72% accurate."="accuracy"), answer="estimate", hint="Distinguish a model estimate from a confirmed clinical diagnosis.", explanation="A predicted probability of 72% is the model's estimate based on the predictors included. It is not a confirmed diagnosis and does not tell us that the model is 72% accurate. Clinical assessment and appropriate diagnostic testing are still required.")),
       recovery_question="Which statistical method is commonly used when the outcome variable has two categories, such as diabetes present or absent?", recovery_choices=c("Binary logistic regression"="logistic","Linear regression"="linear","One-way ANOVA"="anova","Pearson correlation"="pearson"), recovery_answer="logistic")
)

    column(3,
           div(class="card sidebar-card",

                 tags$li("Screen and summarise biomedical data appropriately."),
                 tags$li("Apply probability concepts to estimate health-related risks."),
                 tags$li("Use samples to make inferences about wider populations."),
                 tags$li("Interpret confidence intervals and measures of uncertainty."),
                 tags$li("Interpret p-values and the results of hypothesis tests."),
                 tags$li("Select appropriate statistical methods for different study designs."),

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  current <- reactiveVal(1); unlocked <- reactiveVal(FALSE); show_hint <- reactiveVal(FALSE)
  feedback <- reactiveVal(""); feedback_type <- reactiveVal("info"); attempts <- reactiveVal(0)
  solved <- reactiveVal(integer(0)); complete <- reactiveVal(FALSE)
  score <- reactiveVal(0); recovery_required <- reactiveVal(FALSE); difficulty_locked <- reactiveVal(FALSE)
  target_score <- 21
  output$game_complete <- renderText(if (complete()) "true" else "false")
  outputOptions(output,"game_complete",suspendWhenHidden=FALSE)
  active_question <- reactive({
    c <- cases[[current()]]
    level <- if (is.null(input$difficulty)) "Medium" else input$difficulty
    c$levels[[level]]
  })
  output$main_panel <- renderUI({
    if (complete()) {
      return(div(class="card final-screen",
                 div(style="font-size:54px","🏥"),
                 div(class="specialty","ALL STAGES COMPLETED"),
                 h2("You’ve completed the Medical Statistics Escape Room!"),
                 p("You’ve worked through all seven stages and completed the statistics challenges."),
                 div(class="good-box",h4("Your achievements"),
                     uiOutput("completion_achievements")),
                 div(class="side-stat",strong("Final score: "),score()," points"),
                 fluidRow(column(4,div(class="side-stat",div(class="stat-num",length(solved())),"Stages completed")),
                          column(4,div(class="side-stat",div(class="stat-num",attempts()),"Retries")),
                          column(4,div(class="side-stat",div(class="stat-num",score()),"Points earned"))),
                 actionButton("restart","Restart the escape room",class="btn-primary")))
    }
    c <- cases[[current()]]
    q <- active_question()
    div(class="card",
        div(class="room-map",lapply(seq_along(cases),function(i){
          cls <- if(i %in% solved()) "room-step done" else if(i==current()) "room-step active" else "room-step"
          div(class=cls,paste0(i,". ",c("Records","Screening","Sampling","Evidence","Tests","BMI groups","Logistic")[i]))
        })),
        div(id="readable-case",

        if(current()==2) tagList(

              div(class="screening-table-wrap", tableOutput("screening_table")),
              plotOutput("mosaic_plot",height="420px",width="100%"))),
        if(current()==4) tagList(
          div(class="evidence",h4("Explore the treatment comparison"),

Move them to 35 patients in the new-treatment group and 57 in the standard-treatment group to reproduce the study results, or try other values to see how the contingency table, mosaic plot and chi-squared test change. The remaining patients did not reach the target."),
              sliderInput("new_treatment_success","Patients reaching target with the new treatment (out of 60)",min=0,max=60,value=0,step=1),
              sliderInput("standard_treatment_success","Patients reaching target with the standard treatment (out of 140)",min=0,max=140,value=0,step=1),
              tableOutput("trial_contingency_table"),
              plotOutput("trial_mosaic",height="560px",width="100%"),
              uiOutput("trial_chi_square_output"))),
        if(current()==3) tagList(
          div(class="evidence",h4("Explore a confidence interval for mean systolic blood pressure"),
              p("Explore how the sample mean, sample size and confidence level affect a confidence interval for the population mean systolic blood pressure. The example uses a standard deviation of 15 mmHg, kept constant so you can see how changing the other values affects the interval. The study described above began with 120 patients; adjust the sample-size slider to explore what would happen with different sample sizes."),
              sliderInput("ci_mean","Sample mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",min=110,max=154,value=132,step=1),
              sliderInput("ci_n","Sample size",min=10,max=500,value=120,step=10),

              plotOutput("ci_plot",height="210px"),uiOutput("ci_interpretation"))),
        if(current()==7) tagList(
          div(class="evidence",h4("Explore a logistic regression model"),
              p("Adjust age and BMI to see how the model's estimated probability of Type 2 diabetes changes. Try changing one slider at a time so you can see the effect of each predictor."),
              sliderInput("patient_age","Patient age (years)",min=18,max=90,value=55,step=1),
              sliderInput("patient_bmi","BMI (kg/m²)",min=18,max=45,value=30,step=0.5),
              uiOutput("logistic_output"),plotOutput("logistic_plot",height="500px"))),
        if(unlocked()) div(class="good-box",h4("Stage complete, nice work!"),
                           p(q$explanation),
                           p(strong("Achievement completed: "),c(
                             "Screened and summarised HbA1c data",
                             "Used probability to understand diabetes risk",
                             "Estimated population values from patient samples and interpreted confidence intervals",
                             "Evaluated evidence from clinical trials",
                             "Selected appropriate statistical tests",
                             "Recognised when statistical assumptions were violated",
                             "Investigated how BMI and age contribute to estimated diabetes risk"
                           )[current()]),
                           p(c$unlock),
                           p("Points earned: ",if(input$difficulty=="Easy") 1 else if(input$difficulty=="Hard") 3 else 2),

  output$screening_table <- renderTable({
    data.frame(
      `Pre-diabetes\nstatus`=c("Pre-diabetes","No pre-diabetes","Total"),
      `Develops Type 2\ndiabetes`=c(20,5,25),
      `Does not develop\nType 2 diabetes`=c(80,95,175),
      `Total`=c(100,100,200),
      check.names=FALSE
    )
  }, striped=TRUE, bordered=TRUE, spacing="s", rownames=FALSE)
  
  output$mosaic_plot <- renderPlot({
    screening <- matrix(c(20,80,5,95),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,
                        dimnames=list("Pre-diabetes status"=c("Pre-diabetes","No pre-diabetes"),
                                      "Outcome"=c("Develops T2D","No T2D")))
    par(mar=c(5,5,5,2), oma=c(0,0,0,0))
    mosaicplot(screening, color=c("#168b8b","#e8b45b"),
               main="Pre-diabetes status\nand Type 2 diabetes outcome",
               xlab="Pre-diabetes status",ylab="Diabetes outcome",
               las=1,cex.axis=.8,cex.lab=.9,cex.main=1.0,
               off=4, border="white")
  },res=120)
  
  output$trial_contingency_table <- renderTable({
    new_yes <- input$new_treatment_success %||% 0
    standard_yes <- input$standard_treatment_success %||% 0
    data.frame(
      `Treatment group`=c("New treatment","Standard treatment","Total"),
      `Reached HbA1c target`=c(new_yes,standard_yes,new_yes+standard_yes),
      `Did not reach target`=c(60-new_yes,140-standard_yes,200-new_yes-standard_yes),
      `Total`=c(60,140,200),
      check.names=FALSE
    )
  }, striped=TRUE, bordered=TRUE, spacing="s", rownames=FALSE)
  
  output$trial_mosaic <- renderPlot({
    new_yes <- input$new_treatment_success %||% 0
    standard_yes <- input$standard_treatment_success %||% 0
    treatment_data <- matrix(c(new_yes,60-new_yes,standard_yes,140-standard_yes),
                             nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,
                             dimnames=list("Treatment group"=c("New","Standard"),
                                           "HbA1c outcome"=c("Reached","Not reached")))
    par(mar=c(5,6,4,2), mgp=c(2.8,.8,0))
    mosaicplot(treatment_data, color=c("#168b8b","#e8b45b"),
               main="HbA1c outcome by treatment group",
               xlab="Treatment group",ylab="HbA1c outcome",
               las=1,cex.axis=.75,cex.lab=.9,cex.main=1.0,
               off=3,border="white")
  },res=120)
  
  output$trial_chi_square_output <- renderUI({
    new_yes <- input$new_treatment_success %||% 0
    standard_yes <- input$standard_treatment_success %||% 0
    tab <- matrix(c(new_yes,60-new_yes,standard_yes,140-standard_yes),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE)
    if(any(rowSums(tab)==0) || any(colSums(tab)==0)) {
      return(div(class="hint-box","The chi-squared test cannot be calculated when a row or column total is zero. Adjust the sliders to include both outcome categories."))
    }
    test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab,correct=FALSE))
    if(any(test$expected < 5)) {
      return(div(class="hint-box","Some expected cell frequencies are below 5. Consider Fisher's exact test rather than relying on the chi-squared approximation."))
    }
    div(class="side-stat",
        div(class="muted","CHI-SQUARED TEST: TREATMENT AND HbA1c OUTCOME"),
        p(paste0("Chi-squared statistic: ",round(unname(test$statistic),2))),
        p(paste0("Degrees of freedom: ",unname(test$parameter))),
        p(paste0("p-value: ",format.pval(test$p.value,digits=3,eps=0.001))),
        p(if(test$p.value<0.05) "At the 5% significance level, there is evidence that the proportion reaching the HbA1c target differs between the two treatment groups." else "At the 5% significance level, there is insufficient evidence that the proportion reaching the HbA1c target differs between the two treatment groups."),
        p(class="small-note","The test assesses whether treatment group and reaching the HbA1c target are associated. It does not by itself establish clinical importance or prove causation."))
  })
  
  output$ci_plot <- renderPlot({
    n <- input$ci_n %||% 120
    conf <- input$ci_conf %||% .95
    sd <- 15
    estimate <- input$ci_mean %||% 132
    critical <- qt(1-(1-conf)/2,df=n-1)
    margin <- critical*sd/sqrt(n)
    lo <- estimate-margin
    hi <- estimate+margin
    par(mar=c(4,2,2,1))
    plot(NA,xlim=c(estimate-20,estimate+20),ylim=c(.7,1.3),
         yaxt="n",xlab="Mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",ylab="",
         main=paste0(round(conf*100),"% confidence interval for the population mean"),bty="n")
    segments(lo,1,hi,1,lwd=5,col="#168b8b")
    segments(lo,.94,lo,1.06,lwd=2,col="#168b8b")
    segments(hi,.94,hi,1.06,lwd=2,col="#168b8b")
    points(estimate,1,pch=19,cex=1.5,col="#183153")
    axis(1)
    legend("topright",legend=c("Sample mean","Confidence interval"),
           pch=c(19,NA),lty=c(NA,1),lwd=c(NA,4),col=c("#183153","#168b8b"),bty="n",cex=.8)
  },res=96)
  
  output$ci_interpretation <- renderUI({
    n <- input$ci_n %||% 120
    conf <- input$ci_conf %||% .95
    sd <- 15
    estimate <- input$ci_mean %||% 132
    critical <- qt(1-(1-conf)/2,df=n-1)
    margin <- critical*sd/sqrt(n)
    div(class="side-stat",
        div(class="muted","CURRENT ESTIMATE"),
        p(paste0("Sample mean: ",estimate," mmHg")),
        p(paste0("Confidence interval: ",round(estimate-margin,1)," to ",round(estimate+margin,1)," mmHg")),
        p(paste0("Width: ",round(2*margin,1)," mmHg | n = ",n," | confidence level = ",round(conf*100),"% | standard deviation = 15 mmHg"))
    )
  })
  
  output$logistic_output <- renderUI({
    age <- input$patient_age %||% 55
    bmi <- input$patient_bmi %||% 30
    log_odds <- -8 + .04*age + .12*bmi
    probability <- 1/(1+exp(-log_odds))
    div(class="side-stat",
        div(class="muted","PREDICTED PROBABILITY"),
        div(class="stat-num",paste0(round(probability*100,1),"%")),
        p(paste("Age:",age,"years | BMI:",bmi,"kg/m²"))
    )
  })
  
  output$logistic_plot <- renderPlot({
    age <- input$patient_age %||% 55
    bmi <- seq(18,45,by=.5)
    log_odds <- -8 + .04*age + .12*bmi
    probability <- 1/(1+exp(-log_odds))
    plot(bmi,probability*100,type="l",lwd=3,col="#168b8b",
         xlab="BMI (kg/m²)",ylab="Predicted probability (%)",
         main=paste("Model at age",age),ylim=c(0,100))
    abline(h=50,lty=2,col="#d65b4a")
  },res=96)
  
  output$feedback_ui <- renderUI({msg<-feedback();if(!nzchar(msg))return(NULL);if(feedback_type()=="success")div(class="good-box",msg) else if(feedback_type()=="error")div(class="bad-box",msg) else p(msg)})
  output$progress_ui <- renderUI({
    n <- length(solved()); sc <- score()
    tagList(
      div(class="side-stat",div(class="muted","YOUR PROGRESS"),
          div(class="stat-num",paste0(n," / ",length(cases))),
          div(class="progress",div(class="progress-bar",style=paste0("width:",100*n/length(cases),"%;height:100%")))),
      div(class="side-stat",div(class="muted","YOUR SCORE (AIM FOR 21)"),

          div(class="progress",div(class="progress-bar",style=paste0("width:",min(100,100*sc/target_score),"%;height:100%"))),
          if(sc >= target_score) strong("You’ve reached the points target! Keep going.")),

  })
  output$achievement_checklist <- renderUI({
    completed <- c(
      1 %in% solved(), 2 %in% solved(), 3 %in% solved(), 3 %in% solved(),
      4 %in% solved(), 5 %in% solved(), 6 %in% solved(), 7 %in% solved()
    )
    labels <- c(
      "Screened and summarised HbA1c data",
      "Used probability to understand diabetes risk",
      "Estimated population values from patient samples",
      "Interpreted confidence intervals",
      "Evaluated evidence from clinical trials",
      "Selected appropriate statistical tests",
      "Recognised when statistical assumptions were violated",
      "Investigated how BMI and age contribute to estimated diabetes risk"
    )
    tagList(lapply(seq_along(labels), function(i) {
      tags$div(class="achievement-item",
               tags$input(type="checkbox", checked=if(completed[i]) "checked" else NULL,
                          disabled="disabled", id=paste0("achievement_",i)),
               tags$label(`for`=paste0("achievement_",i), labels[i]))
    }))
  })
  output$completion_achievements <- renderUI({
    labels <- c(
      "Screened and summarised HbA1c data",
      "Used probability to understand diabetes risk",
      "Estimated population values from patient samples",
      "Interpreted confidence intervals",
      "Evaluated evidence from clinical trials",
      "Selected appropriate statistical tests",
      "Recognised when statistical assumptions were violated",
      "Investigated how BMI and age contribute to estimated diabetes risk"
    )
    tags$ul(lapply(labels, tags$li))
  })
  observeEvent(input$hint,show_hint(TRUE))
  observeEvent(input$submit,{
    if(complete()||unlocked())return()
    c<-cases[[current()]]
    if(recovery_required()){
      if(is.null(input$recovery_answer)||!nzchar(input$recovery_answer)){feedback("Pick an answer for the recovery question.");feedback_type("error");return()}
      if(identical(input$recovery_answer,c$recovery_answer)){recovery_required(FALSE);feedback("Recovery question complete. You can now try the main question again.");feedback_type("success");updateRadioButtons(session,"recovery_answer",selected=character(0));updateRadioButtons(session,"answer",selected=character(0))} else {feedback("Not quite. Have another look at the evidence and try again.");feedback_type("error")}
      return()
    }
    q<-active_question()
    if(is.null(input$answer)||!nzchar(input$answer)){feedback("Pick an answer first.");feedback_type("error");return()}
    difficulty_locked(TRUE)
    if(identical(input$answer,q$answer)){
      unlocked(TRUE);pts<-if(input$difficulty=="Easy")1 else if(input$difficulty=="Hard")3 else 2;score(score()+pts);feedback("That’s right! Achievement completed.");feedback_type("success");solved(unique(c(solved(),current())))
    } else {
      attempts(attempts()+1)
      penalty <- if(input$difficulty=="Easy") 1 else if(input$difficulty=="Hard") 3 else 2
      score(max(0,score()-penalty))
      recovery_required(TRUE)
      feedback(paste0("That’s not quite right. ",penalty,
                      " point",if(penalty==1) "" else "s",
                      " deducted for the selected difficulty (score cannot fall below zero). ",
                      "Answer the recovery question before trying the main question again."))
      feedback_type("error")
    }
  })
  observeEvent(input$next_room,{req(unlocked());if(current()<length(cases)){current(current()+1);unlocked(FALSE);show_hint(FALSE);feedback("");feedback_type("info");recovery_required(FALSE);difficulty_locked(FALSE);updateRadioButtons(session,"answer",selected=character(0));updateRadioButtons(session,"recovery_answer",selected=character(0));updateSelectInput(session,"difficulty",selected="Medium")}else complete(TRUE)})
  observeEvent(input$restart,{current(1);unlocked(FALSE);show_hint(FALSE);feedback("");feedback_type("info");attempts(0);solved(integer(0));complete(FALSE);score(0);recovery_required(FALSE);difficulty_locked(FALSE);updateRadioButtons(session,"answer",selected=character(0));updateRadioButtons(session,"recovery_answer",selected=character(0));updateSelectInput(session,"difficulty",selected="Medium")})
}
